seo.title: Karmic tail 12 10 16 compatibility: Hanged Man, Wheel and Tower
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 10 16 compatibility: the Hanged Man, the Wheel and the Tower, and why this couple decides long before it speaks, as the Arabian Nights show.

title: Karmic tail 12-10-16 in compatibility: a thousand and one nights for two
short: The Hanged Man, the Wheel of Fortune and the Tower form a tail that only a couple can have: in a personal destiny matrix the road to the Tower as the main task never begins with the Hanged Man. The answer to the riddle fits into one sentence: this couple makes its main decision long before it says it out loud. The two hold on to each other through a deferred "to be continued", live in circles where the same scene comes back again and again, and learn the hardest thing of all: to take apart the old fortress each of them once built out of pain, while it still stands between them.

sections.h2: "I will not slay her until I have heard the rest of her tale"
paragraphs: The story begins with two betrayals. Two kings, the brothers Shahryar and Shah Zaman, discover that their wives are unfaithful and leave their palaces to wander the world. By the sea they meet an Ifrit who carries a captive woman with him. She describes for herself how he keeps her: he "put me into a casket and set the casket in a coffer and to the coffer he affixed seven strong padlocks of steel and deposited me on the deep bottom of the sea that raves" (here and below the Nights are quoted in Richard Burton's translation). While the Ifrit sleeps, the captive takes the brothers' seal rings and shows them a string on which five hundred and seventy rings already hang. She draws the moral herself: "whatso woman willeth the same she fulfilleth however man nilleth".

The brothers take comfort: "there hath happened to him a greater mishap than that which befel us", and they go home. Shahryar has his wife put to death and sets up a routine: a new bride every night, an execution every morning. Three years pass this way, until the Wazir who carries out the sentences can find no more girls in the city.

Then the Wazir's elder daughter, Shahrazad, who "had perused the books, annals and legends of preceding Kings", asks to be given to the King. She explains her reckoning to her father in one sentence: "either I shall live or I shall be a ransom for the virgin daughters of Moslems". She tells her younger sister, Dunyazad, to ask for a story during the night. The sister asks, and Shahrazad begins the tale of the Trader and the Jinni.

At dawn the tale breaks off mid-sentence, and for the first time the book uses a formula it will repeat about a thousand times: "And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say." Her sister praises the story, and Shahrazad answers: "What is this to that I could tell thee on the coming night, were I to live and the King would spare me?" And the King says to himself: "By Allah, I will not slay her, until I shall have heard the rest of her tale."

Then comes a morning worth reading slowly. The King goes to his audience hall, "and the Wazir went up with his daughter's shroud under his arm". The father has brought a shroud for his daughter. Until evening the King "promoted this and deposed that" and told the Wazir nothing.

That single day and night already holds the whole of the 12-10-16 tail. The night belongs to the Hanged Man: the sentence hangs but is not carried out. The day belongs to the Wheel: someone is raised, someone is brought down, and in the evening it all starts again. Behind both stands the thing nobody touches: the King's vow, a fortress built after the betrayal. That is the Tower, the main task, and it is the reason the wheel keeps turning.

The tale hands out its roles by sex; the tail does not. In a real couple either partner can be the storyteller, and either can have a vow of their own. More often each has half of both: one keeps the interest alive, the other keeps the door shut, and in another situation they swap places.

sections.h2: Clues in the numbers: a tail no single person has
paragraphs: The first clue is an impossibility. In a personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the main task plus the centre of the chart. If the main task is the Tower, 16, the entry can never be 12, whatever the centre. A person can have the Tower as the main task in only one tail, 21-10-16, and the centre of such a chart is always the Hierophant.

Lay the two tails side by side and the secret shows through. A 12-10-16 couple gets the same Wheel and the same Tower as a person with the 21-10-16 tail, and the same Hierophant in the centre. Only the entry changes: instead of the World, where everything comes at once and whole, there is the Hanged Man, where everything comes later. For one person this plot starts from fullness. For two it starts from a pause.

The second clue is what stands between the Hanged Man and the Tower. In couples it is almost always the Wheel: the 12-19-16 triple, with the Sun in the Wheel's place, is twenty times rarer, 0.058% of couples against 1.13%.

The third clue is the make-up of the tail. 12-10-16 occurs in roughly one couple in 89 (1.13%, 32nd of the 97 couple tails), and it is nearly always assembled from the same two personal tails. In 98% of these couples one partner has the personal tail 18-6-6 (The Moon, The Lovers, The Lovers) and the other has 21-4-10 (The World, The Emperor, The Wheel of Fortune). Another 2% come from the personal tails 3-13-10 and 9-15-6. Two 6-14-8 tails can also produce it, but so rarely that the share rounds down to zero.

Here is how it works for the dates 14.10.1975 and 04.07.1975. For the first date the day is 14, the month 10, the year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. The main task is 14 + 10 + 22 = 46 → 4 + 6 = 10, the centre 14 + 10 + 22 + 10 = 56 → 11, the entry 10 + 11 = 21, the middle 21 + 10 = 31 → 4: the personal tail 21-4-10. For the second date we have 4, 7 and 22, the main task 33 → 6, the centre 39 → 12, the entry 6 + 12 = 18, the middle 18 + 6 = 24 → 6: the personal tail 18-6-6. Each point of the couple is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices:

The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the personal middles, 4 + 6. For these dates the couple's centre is 11 + 12 = 23 → 5, the Hierophant, and the couple's values card is 15, the Devil.
What each card is made of is a clue in itself.

ul: **The Hanged Man** of the couple is, in 98% of cases, the sum of the World and the Moon, 21 + 18. A whole world told at night: there is no more exact description of what Shahrazad does. The same card also sits on the "Common language" point in the "Relationship and common language" sphere, so it appears twice in the couple's reading.
**The Wheel** is the sum of the personal middles, and in 98% of cases these are the Emperor of one partner and the Lovers of the other, 4 + 6. Power and choice, added together, begin to turn.
**The Tower** is always the exact sum of the two personal main tasks, and almost always these are the Wheel of Fortune of one partner and the Lovers of the other, 10 + 6.

**The Hierophant** in the centre is assembled, in 98% of these couples, from the centres of the personal charts: Strength in one and the Hanged Man in the other, 11 + 12 = 23 → 5. So the Hanged Man already lives inside one of the two, in that person's comfort zone.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, The Hanged Man: a knife stopped by the dawn
paragraphs: Shahrazad does not break off her first night just anywhere. Her first tale is about a trader who ate some dates and threw away the stones, and a stone killed the son of a Jinni. The Jinni raises his sword; the trader asks for a delay until the head of the new year so that he can settle his debts, and a year later he comes back of his own accord: he "took his shroud under his arm and bade farewell to his people, his neighbours and all his kith and kin, and went forth despite his own nose". Three old men buy his life. Each tells the Jinni a story, and for a marvellous story the Jinni promises "a third of his blood". The very first tale of the book is the frame in miniature: time is bought by delay, and life is bought by a story.

Dawn finds Shahrazad in the middle of the first old man's story. His wife, a sorceress, has turned his son into a calf, and on "the Great Festival of Allah" he must slaughter the finest beast. The night's last words are: "I went up to the calf, knife in hand". In a footnote Burton explains that the Great Festival is the Id al-Kabir, the "Festival of the Kurbán" (sacrifice). It is kept in memory of Abraham's knife, stopped above his son. The first night of the book ends with a knife raised over a son on the feast of sacrifice, and the dawn stops it just as it stops the sword above the storyteller herself.

Among Waite's divinatory meanings for the Hanged Man is the word "sacrifice", and he sums up the card in the formula "life in suspension, but life and not death". The thousand nights are built exactly that way: the execution is not cancelled, it is postponed, and inside the postponement life goes on: conversations, children, three years of marriage.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its common language. Here that language is strikingly shared. The King wants to hear the end. Shahrazad wants to see the morning. It is one wish seen from two ends: that the story should go on. The Hanged Man looks at the world upside down, and the couple sees the same pause from opposite sides: for one it is curiosity, for the other it is rescue.

In a real couple this language is easy to recognise. The important conversation is always "let's talk tomorrow". The decision about moving, about the wedding, about children, about what really happened three years ago, hangs in the air, and it hangs gently, without quarrels, because that feels kinder. The evening is built like a series: we'll finish watching, we'll finish talking, the main thing can wait. Lisovskaya writes of the Hanged Man in a couple that such people take a long time to enter a relationship and need a push from outside to take the decisive step. In the tale that push sits at the foot of the couch, and her name is Dunyazad. Every night the conversation is opened not by Shahrazad and not by the King but by the third: "Allah upon thee, O my sister, recite to us some new story, delightsome and delectable, wherewith to while away the waking hours of our latter night." A real couple has its own Dunyazad, a friend, a shared project, a circumstance, who asks the question the two do not ask each other.

Lisovskaya describes the minus side of the Hanged Man as the path of sacrifice: everything for the other, nothing for oneself, one partner holding the relationship together with all their strength and unable to leave. That is Shahrazad at the moment the tale stops being a game: every night she has to be interesting again, or in the morning there is the shroud. In a couple it looks peaceful. One partner keeps trying, inventing, entertaining, reading the other's mood, while the other takes it for granted and keeps the decision to themselves.

This point has a reverse side too: it stands on the line of tasks, so the couple's wish easily turns into its resistance. As long as there is another episode, there is no need to write the ending. The pause that saved the two on the first night becomes, by the hundredth, a way of not speaking.

And yet the Hanged Man holds what leads out of this circle. Benebell Wen writes: "There is a component of grace to the card. The Seeker must show grace to his or her condemners." Shahrazad does not argue with the King about his vow and does not accuse him. She comes not with a verdict on his verdict but with a story. That is the strength of a 12-10-16 couple: the ability not to storm the other's fortress head-on.

sections.h2: Middle of the task, The Wheel of Fortune: a morning with a shroud under the arm
paragraphs: The strangest thing in the Thousand and One Nights is not the jinn but the repetition. The same formula, the dawn, the "permitted say", the sister's praise, "were I to live", the King's decision to wait, comes back night after night. A thousand and one nights is almost two years and nine months. Before Shahrazad the King had been killing for three years. Her stories lasted three years as well: at the end, in Burton's text, the King tells his brother what had befallen him with Shahrazad "during the past three years". The Wheel makes a full turn: the same span of time, the same king, the same bedchamber, only now there are stories instead of executions.

By day the wheel turns quite literally: the King "promoted this and deposed that". For the courtiers this is the Wheel of Fortune in its purest form: raised today, brought down tomorrow. And at night the same man finds himself inside someone else's wheel, held by a plot that does not belong to him.

Shahrazad knew the law of the wheel in advance. Her first words in the book are a verse with which she comforts her father: "Tell whoso hath sorrow / Grief never shall last: / E'en as joy hath no morrow / So woe shall go past." Waite says the Wheel stands "for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life". Wen compares it to "the mathematical concept of the unit circle", to sine and cosine, "revealing the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs", and calls the wheel "the mandala of the tarot, encompassing the whole of the teachings in the Major Arcana". Both descriptions fit the book literally: the frame holds all the tales, and life inside it runs as a sine wave, danger peaking at dawn, relief in the evening, and round again.

The middle of the task is how the couple travels from its shared wish to its main task. For 12-10-16 that path is not straight but circular. Lisovskaya sees cyclicity in the couple's Wheel: rises and crises follow one another, and what has to be accepted is the change itself, rather than fighting it. She describes the minus side as a swing between silence and conflict, and the feeling that it is hard to be together and yet something holds them. In the tale that something has a name: an unfinished story.

In a real couple the wheel shows in repetitions. The same quarrel at the same time of year. The same evening in which one waits and the other tells. Every reconciliation is like a new night: relief, tenderness, the promise to talk tomorrow. The Wheel gives the couple rhythm and a sense of destiny, which is its plus side; Lisovskaya writes of the feeling of a fated meeting. But the rhythm has a price: every turn is bought with fresh effort, and the wheel makes no decisions.

In a footnote to the ending Burton keeps a spare turn of the wheel. In the French version of Trébutien the King replies at the end: "C'est assez; qu'on lui coupe la tête, car ces dernières histoires surtout m'ont causé un ennui mortel" ("Enough; off with her head, for these last stories above all have bored me to death"), and Burton adds that "this reading is found in some of the MSS." It sounds like a joke, but it is accurate: a union held together only by suspense will one day run into boredom. The Wheel turns both ways.

The numbers show what drives this wheel. The couple's middle is the sum of the personal middles, and almost always these are the Emperor of one partner and the Lovers of the other. Power and choice. While power postpones the decision and the choice is not made, both forces go into spinning.

sections.h2: Main task, The Tower: a fortress built on one sentence
paragraphs: Behind all this turning stands a structure that no one touches for a thousand nights. In Burton's translation its foundation is fully visible. On his return Shahryar swears to marry a new wife every night and put her to death the next morning "to make sure of his honour": "For," said he, "there never was nor is there one chaste woman upon the face of earth."

The whole tower rests on one sentence. And the King drew that sentence not from his own life but from someone else's: from the Ifrit's captive and her rings. The brothers look at the Ifrit's misfortune and take comfort that he is worse off. Someone else's catastrophe becomes, for the King, a law about everyone. Wen describes exactly this kind of Tower in its reversed position: "the Seeker relied on false impressions made by others, and as a result will now feel a jolt."

The main task of a couple is the point Lisovskaya reads mostly through its minus side: what the couple fails at and what it has to learn. Among the Tower's tasks she puts first the collapse of an invented image of the partner. In a 12-10-16 couple this image is invented before they meet. Each brings a tower from the past: "everyone leaves", "nobody can be trusted", "I am loved as long as I am interesting". The partner has done nothing yet, but the sentence has already been passed, and every morning it is postponed again.

Waite calls the Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". This couple foresees its catastrophe every morning, and it never comes. Something else falls: the fortress itself, and it falls quietly.

At the end Shahrazad has three sons. She brings them to the King, "one walking, one crawling and one sucking", and asks him to lift the sentence for the children's sake. The King weeps, strains the boys to his bosom and answers: "By Allah, O Shahrazad, I pardoned thee before the coming of these children, for that I found thee chaste, pure, ingenuous and pious!" (Burton's translation).

Here is the answer to the riddle of the tail. "There never was nor is there one chaste woman" collapses under "I found thee chaste". That is the collapse of the invented image: not a lightning bolt but an admission. And the main thing is this: the Tower fell long before the ending. The King had pardoned her earlier, the book does not say when, but until the last night nobody said so. The wheel kept turning by inertia, the sentence kept hanging, and the storyteller kept earning her morning every night.

A 12-10-16 couple makes its main decision before it says it out loud. One partner stopped testing long ago, the other stopped being afraid long ago, yet both live as if the exam were still going on. The task of the Tower is not to wait for the blow but to say aloud: the fortress is no longer needed.

Shahrazad's last words in the book also strike at the foundation of the tower. She reminds the King that the Kings of the Chosroës before him suffered worse mishaps, "and in this is all sufficient warning for the man of wits". The very argument with which the brothers once consoled themselves by the sea, that others have had it worse, she turns the other way round. From someone else's misfortune you can derive a law about everyone, or you can understand that your misfortune is not the only one and that no law follows from it.

Music remembers this Tower too. The finale of Rimsky-Korsakov's suite "Scheherazade" was at first titled "Festival at Baghdad. The Sea. The Ship Breaks against a Cliff Surmounted by a Bronze Horseman"; later the composer removed the titles of the movements. The ship breaks up, yet the suite ends not with the wreck but with the storyteller's quiet violin.

The numbers add a final clue. The couple's Tower is almost always made of the Wheel of Fortune of one partner and the Lovers of the other, their personal main tasks. In their own lives one is learning to accept the turns of fate, the other to choose. Together they bring down what neither turning nor choosing could touch alone.

sections.h2: The atmosphere inside the couple, The Hierophant: marriage, captivity and mercy
paragraphs: The centre of a 12-10-16 couple is the Hierophant in every case without exception. This is not a coincidence but arithmetic: when the couple's main task is the Tower, the centre can only be the Hierophant or Temperance. In 3-10-16 couples it is almost always Temperance; in 12-10-16 couples it is only the Hierophant.

Waite's list of divinatory meanings for the Hierophant reads like a summary of the Thousand and One Nights: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness". In the book these words come almost in order. First a marriage that is in fact captivity and servitude. Then mercy. And only after mercy comes alliance: at the end, in Burton's text, the King sends for "the Kazis and Olema", the judges and the scholars of the law, who marry the couples, and "the contracts were written out". For three years the two have lived as husband and wife, yet only now does Burton call Shahrazad the King's "betrothed", "i.e. whom he intended to marry with regal ceremony".

The atmosphere is what happens between the partners and is not put on show. Here it is the rules of speech. "Permitted say" is in Arabic "Kalám al-mubáh", and Burton explains it as speech "allowed or permitted to her by the King, her husband". Mubāḥ is a term of Islamic law: it names what is permissible, neither commanded nor forbidden. For a thousand nights the two live by a statute: at night one may tell stories, in the morning one must fall silent; the tales may be spoken of, the vow may not.

In a real couple this is recognisable at once. The two have an unspoken list: we don't talk about this in front of the family, this only on holiday, the past never. The rules hold the household together the way they held Shahryar's bedchamber. Lisovskaya sees both sides in the couple's Hierophant. On the plus side these are two people who are also friends: they can trust each other, and their conversation never runs dry. On the minus side the same conversation turns into upbringing: one keeps explaining to the other how things should be done, and the house echoes with an endless "it's all wrong".

Wen says the Hierophant "is about the pedagogy of wisdom and divine knowledge", and the Thousand and One Nights is perhaps the longest lesson in literature. Shahrazad had read the annals and legends of kings; at the end, in Burton's text, she herself calls her stories "admonitory instances of the men of yore". Even the first story in the book is a lesson, and it is not she who tells it. Her father, trying to talk her out of her plan, tells her the Tale of the Bull and the Ass to keep her away from the King. One parable forbids; the thousand that follow set free.

That is the danger of this centre. Shahrazad remade her partner, but she did not preach at him: her lessons are always about others, about traders, fishermen and kings. A 12-10-16 couple loses that lightness when the tale turns into a lecture, when one partner brings up the other in plain words and waits for them to improve.

Wen has a thought about the Hierophant that might have been written for the Ifrit and his coffer: "a person should never assume he or she knows better than another and therefore try to 'protect' or shield someone else from knowledge. We are not the keeper of others." The Ifrit locked up his captive so that she would remain chaste. The King put his wives to death to make sure of his honour. Both keepers lost. A couple's rules work as long as they are an agreement and not a lock.

sections.h2: The couple's values: a chain or a choice
paragraphs: The couple's values are the point that records what the union exists for. For the 12-10-16 tail there is a fork here, split almost exactly in half: 50.9% of these couples have the Devil, 49.1% the Lovers.

Among Waite's meanings for the Devil is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". The value of these couples is a bond both partners feel as fate: it holds more strongly than any argument. Its shadow shows in the same scene at the end. Shahrazad asks for mercy for the children's sake, which means she holds the King with something stronger than a story. Among the Devil's tasks Lisovskaya names the wish to hold a partner with something stronger than feeling, a child, money, position, and her main thought about the Devil in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. The Ifrit with his seven padlocks learned that the hard way.

Waite gives the Lovers as "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome". The value of these couples is a choice made freely. The King's answer is about exactly that: the children were not needed, the decision had been made earlier, and it was made from who he had come to know she was. A chain or a choice: one tail gives two answers to the question "why are we together", and the couple's reading shows which of them the two have drawn.

sections.h2: How a 12-10-16 couple steps out of the circle
paragraphs: The tail predicts neither a break-up nor a happy ending. It shows where the two keep their key. The plot is changed not by magic but by speech.

ul: **Say out loud what has already been decided.** The main question for this couple is not "what happens next?" but "what did we decide long ago and never say?". A pardon that nobody mentions goes on working like a sentence.

**Name the vows.** Each partner has a sentence of their own in the "there never was nor is" mould: "nobody can be trusted", "I'll be left", "I'm needed as long as I'm useful". It is worth asking whether it was said about the present partner or about someone they never even saw.

**Allow the series to end.** The one who tells the stories can, for once, stop trying, and find that the morning comes anyway. The one who listens can stop "promoting this and deposing that" and say that the story has already convinced them.

**Tell a lesson from a tale.** The Hierophant in the centre gives the couple plenty to talk about; the talk goes sour when it turns into upbringing. Each speaks about themselves instead of teaching the other through other people's examples.
**Rewrite the statute.** Go through the unspoken list of "we don't talk about that" together: what in it protects the home, and what merely stands guard.

**Make the agreement afterwards, not under the sword.** In the book the marriage contract is written after the pardon. Agreements made out of fear hold like a lock; agreements made afterwards hold like a union.

paragraphs: The tale is a metaphor, even though the King in it really does put people to death. If, in a real relationship, one partner threatens the other, this is not a task of the tail and not a reason to endure for the sake of "to be continued": it is danger, and the right step is to call a local emergency number and seek help from people close by and from a psychologist.

In its strong version a 12-10-16 couple can do what few manage: wait without pressing, and change each other without preaching. The wheel does not vanish after the ending: in Burton's text the two brother kings abide "each ruling a day in turn", but now it is a rota, not a sentence. And Shahryar's last command in the book is to summon scribes and copyists and have them write down all that had befallen him with his wife, "first and last". It came to thirty volumes. A thousand and one nights lived as a postponement become a book with an ending, and that is its happiness.

intro: Three cards, three roles in the couple's task:

ul: **Entry to the task: 12, The Hanged Man.** What the couple wants together and the language it speaks: to wait, not to put a full stop, to leave the important thing for tomorrow. This wish holds the two together, and the same wish resists the ending.
**Middle of the task: 10, The Wheel of Fortune.** How the couple walks the path: in circles. Rise and fall, alarm and relief, and a scene played a year ago comes back almost word for word.
**Main task: 16, The Tower.** What the couple has to learn: to dismantle false supports, the vows of "never again" and a ready-made image of the partner, invented before the two even met.
**The atmosphere inside the couple: 5, The Hierophant, in every such couple without exception.** Rules, lessons, "the proper way" and an unspoken list of what may be talked about.

intro: There is a book in which this tail is played out from the first night to the last. Everyone who has heard the words "The Thousand and One Nights" knows how it begins. Few read the ending, and that is exactly where the answer lies.

faq.q: Is the 12-10-16 tail a sign of bad compatibility?
faq.a: No. The couple's matrix gives no percentages and passes no verdicts. The tail describes a task: how the two enter it, how they live through it and what they learn. For a 12-10-16 couple the task is to turn a postponement into a decision and to take apart the vows each of them brought from the past.

faq.q: Does the Tower as the main task predict a break-up?
faq.a: No. Here the Tower is a task, not an event and not a date. The main task is read through what the couple fails at: clinging to an invented image of the partner and to old vows of "never again". The plot of the tail shows that a fortress can fall quietly, from an admission spoken aloud.

faq.q: Why do all couples with this tail have the Hierophant in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the couple's arithmetic works. When the couple's main task is the Tower, the centre can only be the Hierophant or Temperance, and with the Hanged Man at the entry only the Hierophant ever comes up. So the atmosphere of every such couple is the same: rules, lessons and an unspoken list of what may be talked about.

No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 16-10-12 and 10-12-16 never occur, and the engine finds no pair of dates that gives 12-16-10: these three numbers combine only in the order 12-10-16. There are other tails with the Tower as the main task, 3-10-16, 21-10-16 and 12-19-16, but those are different couples with different plots.

faq.q: What does it mean if one of us has the personal tail 18-6-6 and the other 21-4-10?
faq.a: That is the most common road to the 12-10-16 tail: 98% of these couples are built this way. The couple's entry is made of the World and the Moon, the middle of the Emperor and the Lovers, the main task of the Wheel of Fortune and the Lovers. Personal tails are read on their own terms: texts about a personal tail are not carried over to the couple's tail.

faq.q: Who is Shahrazad and who is the King in such a couple?
faq.a: The tail belongs to the couple, not to one person, and its roles do not depend on sex. Usually each partner has both: one guards the interest and fears the morning, the other holds the decision and a vow of their own, and in another situation they swap places.

And behind them the Tower: the King's vow, which nobody touches.
The answer lies in the book's last night, but it can be stated at once: **a 12-10-16 couple makes its main decision long before it says it out loud.**

Decisions about moving, about the wedding, about what really happened long ago hang in the air, gently and without quarrels, because that feels kinder. One partner keeps trying: inventing, entertaining, reading the other's mood. The other takes it for granted and keeps the decision to themselves. The roles do not depend on sex, and the two swap them. But this point stands on the line of tasks, and the couple's wish easily turns into its resistance: **as long as there is another episode, there is no need to write the ending.**

report.h3: A wheel that turns instead of a decision

report: The middle of the task is the Wheel of Fortune, and in the book it shows as repetition. The same formula, the dawn, the "permitted say", "were I to live", the King's decision to wait, comes back about a thousand times. Before Shahrazad the King had been killing for three years; her stories lasted three years as well. The same span of time, the same bedchamber, only now there are stories instead of executions.

In a real couple the wheel shows in scenes that repeat. The same quarrel at the same time of year. A reconciliation like a new night: relief, tenderness, the promise to talk tomorrow. The Wheel gives the couple rhythm and a sense of destiny, but every turn is bought with fresh effort, and the wheel makes no decisions.

In a footnote Burton keeps a spare turn of the wheel. In the French version of Trébutien the King replies at the end: "Enough; off with her head, for these last stories above all have bored me to death", and this reading is found in some manuscripts. It sounds like a joke, but it is accurate: a union held together only by suspense will one day run into boredom.

report.h3: A fortress built on one sentence

report: Behind the wheel stands a structure that no one touches for a thousand nights. Returning home after the betrayal, the King swears to marry a new wife every night and put her to death the next morning: "For," said he, "there never was nor is there one chaste woman upon the face of earth." He drew this from someone else's misfortune: from the Ifrit's captive, kept in a casket inside a coffer under seven steel padlocks on the bottom of the sea, who still gathered 570 strangers' rings. Someone else's catastrophe became a law about everyone.

The couple's main task is the Tower, and above all it is the collapse of an invented image of the partner. In a 12-10-16 couple this image is invented before they meet. Each brings a tower from the past: "everyone leaves", "nobody can be trusted", "I am loved as long as I am interesting". The partner has done nothing yet, but the sentence has already been passed, and every morning it is postponed again.

At the end Shahrazad has three sons, and she asks the King to lift the sentence for the children's sake. The King weeps and answers: "By Allah, O Shahrazad, I pardoned thee before the coming of these children, for that I found thee chaste, pure, ingenuous and pious!" "There never was nor is there one chaste woman" collapses under "I found thee chaste". **The Tower falls not to lightning but to an admission**, and it fell long before the ending. Until the last night, nobody said so.

report.h3: After the pardon, not under the sword

report: At the centre of every such couple stands the Hierophant, and Waite's list of its divinatory meanings reads like a summary of the book: "Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness". First a marriage that is in fact captivity. Then mercy. And only after mercy comes alliance: at the end the judges and scholars of the law are summoned and the marriage contracts are written out. Even the "permitted say" is, in the original, "Kalám al-mubáh", a term of Islamic law for what is permissible. The couple has a statute of its own as well: what may be said, what may not, and the past never. It holds the home together as long as it stays an agreement and not a lock.

ul: **saying out loud what has already been decided**: the couple's main question is not "what happens next?" but "what did we decide long ago and never say?";
naming the vows and checking whether they were made about the present partner or about someone from the past;
for the one who tells the stories, for once not trying; for the one who listens, saying that the story has already convinced them;
making agreements after the fear, not under it.

report: The tale is a metaphor, even though the King in it really does put people to death. If, in a real relationship, one partner threatens the other, this is not a task of the tail but danger: call a local emergency number or crisis line and seek help from people close by and from a psychologist.

In its strong version a 12-10-16 couple can do what few manage: wait without pressing, and change each other without preaching. The King's last command in the book is to have everything that had befallen him with his wife written down, "first and last". A thousand and one nights lived as a postponement become a book with an ending.
